paragraphs.text: See Eze 18:1.
paragraphs.anchor: And the word of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: See on Eze 20:46.
paragraphs.anchor: Set thy face.

paragraphs.text: See Deu 32:2 Amo 7:16. As drops of rain follow one upon another, so do words. Speak thick, speak home, though they forbid thee to drop such vinegar or nitre on their galled conscience. {Mic 2:6; Mic 2:11}
paragraphs.anchor: And drop thy word.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Against the temple, which they so cried up, {Jer 7:4} like so many oyster wives, ad ravim usque.
paragraphs.anchor: Toward the holy places

paragraphs.text: That is misery enough, for all the creatures are soon against such; as a nobleman’s servants draw their swords when their lord once draweth.
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, I am against thee.

paragraphs.text: Who are sometimes wrapped up with the wicked in a common calamity. The husbandman cutteth down his corn and weeds together, but for a different end and purpose. If the righteous also be judged of the Lord, it is that they may not be condemned with the world. {1Co 11:31}
paragraphs.anchor: And will cut off from thee the righteous.

paragraphs.text: Velut eodem contubernio deprehensos. This is repeated for more assurance, because it might seem strange. The Septuagint hath it, The unrighteous and the wicked. The Chaldee, I will make the righteous flee, and destroy the wicked. But the Hebrew verity is as before; neither need we wonder, since the best have their infirmities.
paragraphs.anchor: Seeing then that I will cut off from thee the righteons.

paragraphs.text: And put it in commission; not to return till the circuit ended, till it hath done full execution.
paragraphs.anchor: Have drawn forth my sword.

paragraphs.text: Gemituque et gestu dolorem referas; show greatest grief, such as is deep and downright; sigh till thy buttons fly; or as a travailing woman. Non ut praeficae in funeribus solent.
paragraphs.anchor: Sigh therefore, with the breaking of thy loins.

paragraphs.text: Of the Chaldeans’ coming. This was to the wicked as those knuckles of a man’s hand were afterwards to Belshazzar, to write them their destiny; or as Daniel was to him, to read it unto them. Whenas the righteous man is no whit "afraid of evil tidings, his heart is fixed trusting in the Lord." {Psa 112:7}
paragraphs.anchor: For the tidings.

paragraphs.text: As wax before the fire, which, before the danger, seemed to be made all of steel or adamant. The wicked, when in adversity, are woefully despondent and crest fallen, as was the king of Sodom; {Gen 14:9-11} Manasseh among the bushes; {2Ch 33:12} and others not a few, who in their prosperity seem to face the heavens and to draw the devil himself to a duel.
paragraphs.anchor: And every heart shall melt, &c.

paragraphs.text: The spirits and blood being run to the heart, in that fright to relieve it.
paragraphs.anchor: And all hands shall be feeble.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Shall go into water - that is, they shall bepiss themselves for fear, saith Jerome; they shall be all on a cold sweat, say others; or their knees shall shake, instar aquae tremulae, like trembling water, and knock together, as Belshazzar’s did. {Dan 5:6}
paragraphs.anchor: And all knees shall be weak as water.

paragraphs.text: See on Eze 18:1.
paragraphs.anchor: Again the word.

paragraphs.text: {a} Not only drawn, but sharpened, that it may wound swiftly and deadly; furbished also, that it may the more affray and make the quicker despatch. And that no doubt may be made of it, the ward sword is doubled.
paragraphs.anchor: Ver. 9 A sword, a sword is sharpened.

paragraphs.text: {a} Exacutus et extersus, sharp and clean.

Not if we be in our right minds; for would it not be now a mad mirth, whenas we should be most serious and seek God? See Isa 22:12-14. {See Trapp on "Isa 22:12"} {See Trapp on "Isa 22:13"} {See Trapp on "Isa 22:14"}
paragraphs.anchor: Should we then make mirth?

paragraphs.text: Other judgments forerun the sword, which, when they will not do the deed, the sword will then contemn the rod; that is, it will set at naught whatever those have done, and come furbished and sharpened for the slaughter. See Eze 21:3.
paragraphs.anchor: It contemneth the rod of my son.

paragraphs.text: Nebuchadnezzar, who will therewith lay about him lustily, as Eleazar once did till his hand clave unto the sword, {2Sa 23:10} or as since Scanderbeg, who killed many hundred Turks with his own hand, and fought oft with so much eagerness, that the very blood brake forth at his lips. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: To give it into the hand of the slayer.

paragraphs.text: {a} Turkish History.
While others make mirth, {as Eze 21:10} and are insolent against God. Mourners shall be marked, {Eze 9:4} comforted. {Isa 57:18}
paragraphs.anchor: Cry and howl, son of man.

paragraphs.text: See on Jer 31:19.
paragraphs.anchor: Smite therefore upon thy thigh.

paragraphs.text: Sore and sharp; therefore cry and howl, especially since they are not bettered. Hang heavy weights on rotten boughs, they presently break; the best divination of men is at the parting way. See Eze 21:21.
paragraphs.anchor: Because it is a trial.

paragraphs.text: q.d., What doth this silly rod do here? will they not stoop? will they not put their necks under the yoke of God’s Son? {Eze 21:10} Let me come; I will make them either bow or break, either yield or bleed.
paragraphs.anchor: And what if the sword contemn even the rod?

paragraphs.text: So to show what I will do shortly. {Eze 21:17}
paragraphs.anchor: Smite thy hands together.

paragraphs.text: Doubled and trebled, till it hath made an utter end of this untoward generation.
paragraphs.anchor: Let the sword be doubled the third time.

paragraphs.text: Ferreting and fetching them out of their lurking holes.
paragraphs.anchor: Which entereth into their privy chambers.

paragraphs.text: By this doleful exclamation the prophet venteth himself tanquam coram deformitatem cladis cerneret, {a} as if he had seen the execution.
paragraphs.anchor: Ah! it is made bright.

paragraphs.text: {a} Oecolamp.
This he speaketh to the bright and sharp sword, stirring it up to make impression that way whereunto it was appointed, quocunque occurrent tibires comparatae. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Go thee one way or other.

paragraphs.text: {a} Tremel.
As animating the enemy and rejoicing at thy ruin. {a} Chaldee, I will bring revenge upon revenge;
paragraphs.anchor: I will also smite mine hands together.

paragraphs.text: “ Animumque explesse iuvabit. ”
“And he will help satisfy the spirit.”
{a} Exultat quasi hortator gladii saevientis. He exalts just as I will exhortthe angry sword. - Jerome.
See on Eze 18:1.
paragraphs.anchor: The word of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Pinge duas vias, ut Eze 4:1; by prophetic action draw out two ways, by either of which Nebuehadnezzar may march against Egypt, his present aim, as the great Turk’s now is Italy.
paragraphs.anchor: Appoint thee two wags.

paragraphs.text: All this the Jews heard and slighted, as being infatuated, and so fitted for destruction.
paragraphs.anchor: Choose it at the head of the wag to the city.

paragraphs.text: Either against the one or the other of them - not against both at once, {a} for they were both strong, and Jerusalem was well aware of it - for they had both revolted from Nebuchadnezzar, and one of them was enough at once to undertake.
paragraphs.anchor: And to Judah in Jerusalem the defenced.

paragraphs.text: {a} Ne Hercules quidem contra duos.
Heb., At the mother of the way; ubi via una in ducts bifidata est. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: For the king of Babylon stood at the parting.

paragraphs.text: Without which, and offering sacrifice, the very heathens held it not fit to fight. But this their art of divination was, as one saith of alchymy, Ars falsissima et fallacissima.
paragraphs.anchor: To use divination.

paragraphs.text: Vulg., He mingled his arrows; that is, saith Jerome, he took two arrows, writing upon the one Jerusalem, and upon the other Rabbath. Then, putting them into a quiver together, he took one out, being blindfolded; upon which seeing Jerusalem written, he divined that he should go with success against Jerusalem.
paragraphs.anchor: He made his arrows bright.

paragraphs.text: In which the devil sometimes spake. See Aug., De Civitate Dei, lib. iv. cap. 18.
paragraphs.anchor: He consulted with images.

paragraphs.text: This was much practised by the Roman generals, as by Caesar, when he went against Pompey. {b}
paragraphs.anchor: He looked into the liver.

paragraphs.text: {a} Ubi se via findit in ambas. - Virg.
{b} Lucan.
Heb., Rans; fierce and forward, to lead on their soldiers, let them get off as they could.
paragraphs.anchor: To appoint captains.

paragraphs.text: To storm and take it by an onslaught, and with a general slaughter, non sine barritu militari, vociferatione, et clangore insolenti.
paragraphs.anchor: To open their mouth.

paragraphs.text: The Jews shall believe nothing, till wrath comes upon them to the utmost. They shall laugh at Nebuchadnezzar’s fopperies, and think thee, O Ezekiel, to be little wiser than him; ludificabuntur te, adeoque teipsum, divinationis nefariae, quam de Nebuchadnetzare praedicas, incusabunt; { a} but they shall rue this their madness.
paragraphs.anchor: And it shall be to them as a false divination.

paragraphs.text: But cared not at all to keep them. Lingua iuravi, mens iniurata est. The swore with their mouths but not from the heart. {b}
paragraphs.anchor: To them that have sworn oaths.

paragraphs.text: The perfidy and perjury which they make nothing of. They that harden themselves in any one sin, put God in mind, as it were, of the rest, which he had seemed to have forgotten. {c}
paragraphs.anchor: But he will call to remembrance the iniquity.

paragraphs.text: {a} Jun.
{b} Medea.
{c} Iusiurandum tanquam mantile adhibent quo novae noxae quotidie extergeantur. - Pacuvius.
Your old sins, by an addition of new ones.
paragraphs.anchor: Because ye have made your iniquity.

paragraphs.text: You are scandalous, shameless as Sodom. {Isa 3:9}
paragraphs.anchor: Your sins do appear.

paragraphs.text: Or, Worthy to be wounded to death.
paragraphs.anchor: And thou profane.

paragraphs.text: Zedekiah, who now hath his own told him plainly by a prophet. See the like done, 1Sa 13:13 1Ki 18:18 2Ki 3:13-14. {See Trapp on "1Sa 13:13"} {See Trapp on "1Ki 18:18"} {See Trapp on "2Ki 3:13"} {See Trapp on "2Ki 3:14"}
paragraphs.anchor: Wicked prince.

paragraphs.text: This was a fine linen cloth, wherewith the king’s head used to be bound about, {a} and then the crown was set on.
paragraphs.anchor: Remove the diadem.

paragraphs.text: Our Richard II, when to be deposed, was brought forth crowned and in royal robes. Never, saith the chronicler, was prince so gorgeous with less glory and more grief.
paragraphs.anchor: Take off the crown.

paragraphs.text: Haec non erit haec. This crown or kingdom shall not be as it hath been.
paragraphs.anchor: This shall not be the same.

paragraphs.text: Jeconiah, or, as some will, Christ the King of the Church.
paragraphs.anchor: Exalt him that is low.

paragraphs.text: {b} Zedekiah. Let him not henceforth be the master of a molehill, nor owner of his own liberty. In him let it appear that mortality is but the stage of mutability.
paragraphs.anchor: And abase him that is high.

paragraphs.text: {a} Diadema, of διαδειν circumligare.
{b} Just the same that Cambyses threatened unto Egypt, τα μεν ανω κατω, τα δε κατω ανω. - Herod., lib. ii.

Curvam, curvam, curvam ponam eam, so the Tigurines translate. A crown there shall be still, but such as shall hang on one side of the head, as it were. Princes of the people there were. Those three high priests, Alexander, Aristobulus, and Hircanus, who called themselves kings, had very ill Success.
paragraphs.anchor: I will overturn, overturn, overturn it.

paragraphs.text: Christ the rightful King of Israel. To this text alludeth Nathanael. {Joh 1:49}
paragraphs.anchor: Until he come.

paragraphs.text: Who had likewise rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, and were very injurious to God’s people. See Eze 25:3; Eze 25:6 Zep 2:8-9.
paragraphs.anchor: Concerning the Ammonites.

paragraphs.text: “Tβρις και Mαγνμτας απωλεσε και Kολοφωνα.”
To deal inhumanly with the dead, or to raise thyself upon the Jews’ ruin.
paragraphs.anchor: To bring thee upon the necks of them that are slain.

paragraphs.text: No, but it shall still eat your flesh and drink your blood, till none remaineth.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall I cause it to return?

paragraphs.text: In thine own nest, and on thine own dunghill.
paragraphs.anchor: In the land of thy nativity.

paragraphs.text: Or, Of burning men, Ardelionum, artificum perditionis.
paragraphs.anchor: Into the hand of brutish men.

paragraphs.text: {a} The Ammonites were so rooted out by the Medes and Persians, that besides what we find in the Bible, there is no mention of their name. A type of such as are destroyed for ever in hell, being fuel for that black fire, and eternally forgotten.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou shalt be no more remembered.

paragraphs.text: {a} Saltem cum benedictione. - Polan.
